intro.title: PsyUML — a visual language for case formulation in psychotherapy
intro.tagline: Twenty worked formulation diagrams: what each shows, when to reach for it, and how to draw it — on screen or on paper.
intro.lede: PsyUML is a small, cross-school visual language for drawing a person's inner and relational world as a shareable, plain-language case formulation. This page gathers one worked example of every diagram it can draw, grouped by the question each answers. Every diagram below is a real, rendered model — not a mock-up — and you can open any of them live in the editor.

jobs.label: Read a diagram
jobs.summary: Understand what you are looking at. Each example comes with what it shows, the school it is from, and who it is for.

jobs.label: Draw one on paper
jobs.summary: You do not need this software. Every diagram has step-by-step instructions for sketching it with a client using nothing but pen and paper.

jobs.label: Choose the right one
jobs.summary: Eight families, eight questions. Find the diagram that answers the question you are actually asking.

jobs.label: Use it honestly
jobs.summary: These are thinking aids, not instruments. Co-create them, pace them, keep them the client's, and do not overclaim.

readingGuide: PsyUML diagrams share a small visual grammar. They are monochrome by default — meaning never rides on colour alone, so they survive photocopying, projection and colour-blindness; any colour added is redundant.

Boxes and figures are elements (states, parts, people, resources); lines are typed relationships or transitions, and an arrow's label usually says what triggers it. A marked EXIT or a 'way out' is deliberate — a formulation should show a way forward, not only the trap.

Three audiences, one model: the same formulation can be shown in a detailed clinician view, a plain-language client view, or a minimal picture view. The examples here lean to the clinician-and-client view.
Every diagram carries a text alternative for screen readers, and labels are kept legible by construction.
paperGuide: None of this needs a computer. The diagrams were designed to be hand-drawn with a client, and a sheet co-drawn in the room is often better than a polished print-out — because the person watched it being made and helped make it.

A few cross-cutting habits travel to paper: draw it together rather than presenting it finished; use the person's own words for labels; keep it monochrome (a pencil is fine); and always draw the way out, not just the problem.

Start rough. A formulation is a shared hypothesis you expect to revise — leave room, use pencil, and re-draw as understanding changes. Photograph the final sheet for the notes and let the person keep the original.
Each diagram below has an 'On paper' box with concrete steps. Standard conventions (genogram symbols, 0–100 distress ratings, the three ritual phases) are noted where they matter.
honesty: Unvalidated v0.x. PsyUML is an early, cross-school notation. It supports, and does not replace, professional care, and it does not diagnose.

Therapy-evidence is not diagram-evidence. Some of the therapies these diagrams come from are well-evidenced; that does not mean the diagram itself has been shown to improve outcomes. Most are useful shared heuristics, and the honest note on each says so.

A formulation can harm. It is a hypothesis, not a truth, and seeing one can distress a meaningful minority of people. Co-create it, pace it, check its fit, and keep it the client's to hold, change, or put away.
Some popular 'tools' are left out on purpose. Thought records, the PHQ-9 and the 5 Ps grid are worksheets or questionnaires, not diagrams, so they are out of scope here.

families.title: Field
families.question: Who and what is in the person's world?

families.title: Cycle
families.question: What maintaining loop keeps this going?

families.title: Parts
families.question: What internal multiplicity is in play?

families.title: Pattern
families.question: What recurring procedure repeats — and where's the exit?

families.title: Journey
families.question: What is the trajectory / story over time?

families.title: Change
families.question: What is the treatment direction / what to do?

diagrams.school: Polyvagal-informed / window of tolerance (Porges; Dana; Siegel)
diagrams.oneLiner: Autonomic states stacked as bands, with the transitions between them and a way back to safety.
diagrams.whatItShows: Three horizontal bands — ventral / safe-social at the top, sympathetic / mobilised in the middle, dorsal / shutdown at the bottom — each holding the states a person moves through. Arrows are the transitions, labelled with what triggers them; an EXIT arrow marks the route back toward regulation, so the map always shows a way out, not just the trap.
diagrams.whenToUse: Early in the work, to make a confusing, frightening pattern of arousal feel ordinary and mappable; to spot triggers and to rehearse the way back down toward calm.
diagrams.onPaper: Rule three wide horizontal lanes on a landscape sheet and label them green / amber / red (safe · revved-up · shut-down). Write each state where it belongs, draw arrows for how one becomes another and write the trigger on the arrow, then add one bold arrow back up to safety and name the move that gets you there.
diagrams.evidenceNote: Polyvagal theory is a popular clinical frame, not a settled neuroscience account; the ladder of states is a useful psychoeducational metaphor. The diagram organises a conversation — it is not a measure of autonomic state.

diagrams.school: CBT vicious flower / maintenance cycle; CAT
diagrams.oneLiner: The vicious cycle that keeps a problem going — and where to break it.
diagrams.whatItShows: A closed loop of trigger → thought → feeling → body → behaviour that feeds back on itself (the 'vicious flower' / maintaining cycle) — here the health-anxiety trap, where checking and reassurance-seeking lower anxiety briefly but strengthen the fear. An exit marks where a different move breaks the loop.
diagrams.whenToUse: To make a self-perpetuating problem feel understandable and changeable, and to locate the maintaining behaviour worth dropping or testing.
diagrams.onPaper: Write the trigger at the top and follow the arrows round in a circle — thought, feeling, body, what you do — back to the start, so the loop is visibly closed. Then draw one arrow OUT of the circle and write the experiment or skill that breaks it. Always draw the exit; a loop with no way out is a trap, not a formulation.
diagrams.evidenceNote: Maintenance-cycle formulation underpins evidenced CBT; the diagram itself is a shared heuristic for one hypothesis, not a measure, and a person usually has more than one loop.

diagrams.oneLiner: The inner cast — protectors and exiles — held around the Self, with what protects what.
diagrams.whatItShows: Named parts drawn as figures and grouped by role (managers and firefighters that protect; exiles that carry pain), with containment links showing which protector guards which exile, and a central Self. A contested part can carry a ⚖ marker noting that two schools name it differently, with a short footnote on how they differ.
diagrams.whenToUse: When a person feels 'in two minds', self-critical, or at war inside; to build the stance that every part is trying to help, and to find the protected wound without flooding it.
diagrams.onPaper: Put 'Self' in the middle of the page. Around it, sketch each part as a small figure and label it in the person's own words ('the critic', 'the one who hides'). Draw a loose loop from each protector around the part it guards. Do not force it — add parts as they show up, and let the person rename any of them.
diagrams.evidenceNote: IFS is a manualised model with growing but still limited trial evidence. The map is a co-created picture of experience, not a claim about literal sub-personalities.

diagrams.oneLiner: Schema modes sized by how loud each is right now, with the Healthy Adult as the growth target.
diagrams.whatItShows: The person's schema modes — vulnerable child, angry child, the inner critic / demanding parent, coping modes (compliant surrender, detached protector, overcompensation) and the Healthy Adult — each box sized by how dominant it currently is. The Healthy Adult is the part the work grows.
diagrams.whenToUse: In schema therapy, to name the modes that flip a session, to externalise the critic, and to track the Healthy Adult getting stronger over time.
diagrams.onPaper: List the modes down the page and draw each as a box; make the box bigger the more it runs the show. Put the Healthy Adult somewhere prominent and circle it as the one you are feeding. Re-draw it now and again to watch the sizes shift.
diagrams.evidenceNote: Schema therapy has reasonable trial support for some presentations, and mode work is one of its tools. Box sizes are a clinical impression, not a measurement.

diagrams.oneLiner: Reasonable mind and emotion mind overlapping into wise mind.
diagrams.whatItShows: Two overlapping circles — reasonable mind (cool, logical) and emotion mind (hot, mood-driven) — whose overlap is wise mind, where both are integrated. Items the person recognises are sorted into the left-only, the overlap, or the right-only region. The circles are scaffolding; the lens in the middle is the point.
diagrams.whenToUse: In DBT psychoeducation to teach states of mind, to help a person notice which one they are in, and to practise accessing wise mind in a decision.
diagrams.onPaper: Draw two overlapping circles. Label the left 'reasonable / facts', the right 'emotion / mood', and the lens in the middle 'wise mind'. Sort examples from the person's week into the three zones. The work is recognising the middle, not winning for one side.
diagrams.evidenceNote: DBT is well-evidenced for several presentations; 'states of mind' is one of its teaching metaphors, not a measured construct. The diagram supports a skill, it does not assess one.

diagrams.oneLiner: Young's eighteen early maladaptive schemas, sorted into the five domains, active ones highlighted.
diagrams.whatItShows: All eighteen early maladaptive schemas laid out in their five domains (disconnection & rejection; impaired autonomy; impaired limits; other-directedness; overvigilance & inhibition). The schemas a person endorses are highlighted, so the loaded domains stand out — a structured map rather than a free network.
diagrams.whenToUse: In schema therapy assessment and psychoeducation, to locate a person's active schemas within the model and to plan which to target. Mostly a clinician and teaching surface.
diagrams.onPaper: Rule five columns for the domains and write the schemas under each (a schema-therapy reference sheet helps). Tick or shade the ones that ring true for the person. The clustered ticks show the domains to work on.
diagrams.evidenceNote: The 18-schema / 5-domain structure comes from schema therapy and the Young Schema Questionnaire; this grid is an organiser, not the questionnaire, and endorsement here is clinical, not psychometric.

diagrams.oneLiner: The family across generations plus the wider world — who is close, who is cut off, what supports or drains.
diagrams.whatItShows: People as nodes (a genogram's squares and circles) tied by typed relationship lines — close, conflictual, fused, distant, cut-off — together with an ecomap's links out to the systems around the household (work, school, faith, services), drawn heavier or lighter to show how nourishing or stressful each tie is.
diagrams.whenToUse: To take a relational and intergenerational history at a glance, to see patterns repeat across generations, and to map the resources and stresses in a person's social field.
diagrams.onPaper: Genograms have a standard vocabulary worth keeping: square = male, circle = female, a horizontal line = a couple, verticals drop to children, and double / jagged / dashed lines show close / conflicted / distant ties. Put the index person at the centre, draw at least two generations up, then ring the household and draw lines out to the world around it.
diagrams.evidenceNote: The genogram is a near-universal clinical mapping convention rather than a validated instrument. Family information is sensitive and often contested — record whose account it is.

diagrams.oneLiner: The supports a person can reach for, sorted into kinds.
diagrams.whatItShows: A person's resources gathered and grouped by category — people, skills, values, soothing activities, safe places — each held inside its category, so the soothing system is visible as something that can be grown. It is deliberately strengths-forward.
diagrams.whenToUse: To build the 'other side' of a formulation: when a problem-heavy picture needs balancing, when planning relapse prevention, or when a person cannot recall their supports under stress.
diagrams.onPaper: Make four or five labelled buckets on the page — people · skills · values · soothers · places. Brainstorm into them. Star the two or three the person would actually reach for first, and keep the sheet somewhere findable.
diagrams.evidenceNote: A resource inventory is a practical aid rather than a validated scale. Listing a support is not the same as being able to use it under stress — rehearse the important ones.

diagrams.oneLiner: A body outline marked with where sensations sit and how strong they are.
diagrams.whatItShows: An outline of the body with sensations placed where the person feels them — a tight chest, a heavy gut, buzzing hands — each marked for intensity. It externalises interoception so a feeling can be pointed to rather than only spoken.
diagrams.whenToUse: In somatic, trauma and emotion-focused work to build interoceptive vocabulary, to track activation, and to pace and titrate so a person stays inside their window of tolerance.
diagrams.onPaper: Draw a simple gingerbread outline. Ask 'where do you notice it?' and mark the spot; shade darker or draw bigger where it is stronger. Go slowly — this can stir things up, so keep it gentle and stop if it becomes too much.
diagrams.evidenceNote: Body mapping is a widely used experiential technique, not a diagnostic test. Somatic work can raise arousal; pacing and consent matter more than completeness.

diagrams.oneLiner: Threat, drive and soothing systems, sized by how active each one is.
diagrams.whatItShows: The CFT model of three emotion systems — threat (protect), drive (achieve, pursue) and soothing (rest, connect, content) — drawn as three circles sized by how active each is. An over-large threat circle beside a shrunken soothing one shows, at a glance, the imbalance the work addresses.
diagrams.whenToUse: To explain emotion regulation in CFT, to normalise a threat-dominated system as 'not your fault, and trainable', and to set the direction: grow the soothing system.
diagrams.onPaper: Draw three circles labelled threat · drive · soothing. Make each as big as it feels in the person's life right now (often a huge threat, a tiny soothing). Write what sits in each. The plan is usually visible immediately — feed the small one.
diagrams.evidenceNote: CFT has promising but still developing evidence. The three-circles model is a psychoeducational map; circle sizes are a felt impression, not a measurement of brain systems.

diagrams.school: Attachment (Bowlby; Ainsworth) — generic, not a trademarked programme
diagrams.oneLiner: The caregiver as a base to explore from and a haven to return to — a generic attachment graphic.
diagrams.whatItShows: The attachment pair of functions: a secure base a child ventures out from to explore, and a safe haven they come back to for comfort when distressed, with the caregiver behaviours that support each. It is the generic Bowlby / Ainsworth concept, drawn deliberately as its own graphic.
diagrams.whenToUse: In parenting, caregiver and attachment-informed work to explain the two jobs of a caregiver and to reflect on responses around exploration and comfort.
diagrams.onPaper: Draw a circle. On one side write 'base — support exploration' (watch over me, delight in me, help me); on the other 'haven — welcome my return' (comfort me, organise my feelings). Put the child going out and coming back around it. Talk through real moments against the two halves.
diagrams.evidenceNote: Attachment theory is well-established; this is a generic teaching graphic of its concepts. It is NOT the trademarked Circle of Security® programme — use that name and its materials only with proper training and licence.

diagrams.oneLiner: Life events along a line, with the meanings made of them.
diagrams.whatItShows: Significant events placed in order along a horizontal line, each annotated with the meaning or belief that formed at the time ('I learned I had to be useful to be safe'), so a long history and its through-lines become visible together. A preferred-future column points at where the work is heading.
diagrams.whenToUse: To build a shared longitudinal formulation (the 'how did this come to be' story), to connect early experiences to present patterns, and to hold hope by naming a preferred future.
diagrams.onPaper: Draw a long horizontal line across a landscape sheet. Mark birth at the left and 'now' near the right, leaving room for the future. Put events above the line and, below each, the meaning the person took from it. Leave the right-hand end for where they want to be heading.
diagrams.evidenceNote: A lifeline is a formulation aid, not an assessment. Memory is reconstructive and dates are approximate — it maps a story, not a verified record.

diagrams.oneLiner: A life drawn as a tree — roots, ground, trunk, branches, leaves, fruits — strengths first.
diagrams.whatItShows: A botanical metaphor for a life: roots (where you are from, ancestry), ground (daily life), trunk (skills and values), branches (hopes and dreams), leaves (important people) and fruits (gifts received). It is deliberately strengths-forward and identity-affirming, told before any problem talk.
diagrams.whenToUse: In narrative and collective work — especially with children, groups, and people who have faced adversity or displacement — to re-author identity around strengths and belonging rather than diagnosis.
diagrams.onPaper: Draw a big tree filling the page. Roots = where you come from and who raised you; ground = what you do day to day; trunk = your skills and values; branches = hopes; leaves = people who matter; fruits = what others have given you. Co-draw it — it is a portrait, not an assessment.
diagrams.evidenceNote: The Tree of Life is a widely used narrative-practice methodology with practice-based rather than trial evidence. It is a co-created portrait; let the person hold the pen.

diagrams.oneLiner: The planned steps of treatment in order, with who is responsible for each.
diagrams.whatItShows: Treatment steps laid out as an ordered sequence — for phased trauma work, stabilisation → processing → reconnection — each step attached to the next, optionally showing who does what (client, therapist, wider team). It turns a plan into a visible, sequenced map.
diagrams.whenToUse: To agree and share a treatment plan, to make stepped or phased care explicit, and to keep a long piece of work oriented to where it is now and what comes next.
diagrams.onPaper: Draw a row of boxes left to right, one per step, joined by arrows. Write the task in each box and, underneath, who owns it. Mark where you are now. Keep it short — three to five steps reads better than a flowchart no one revisits.
diagrams.evidenceNote: Phase-based trauma treatment is a widely taught framework with debated specifics; the sequence is a shared plan, not a protocol guarantee. Plans change — re-draw as the work moves.

diagrams.school: Psychodynamic — Malan's two triangles (Malan; Menninger; Ezriel)
diagrams.oneLiner: Defence, anxiety and hidden feeling, traced across self, others and the therapist.
diagrams.whatItShows: Malan's classic pairing: the Triangle of Conflict (a hidden feeling, the anxiety it raises, and the defence against it) linked to the Triangle of Person (how the same pattern plays out with current others, past figures, and the therapist in the room). It is a clinician's formulation aid, not a client handout.
diagrams.whenToUse: In psychodynamic and brief-dynamic work to formulate a recurring conflict and to spot it live in the transference — a teaching and supervision staple.
diagrams.onPaper: Draw two triangles side by side. Left (conflict): defence at one corner, anxiety at another, the warded-off feeling at the third. Right (person): others, past, therapist. Note how a defence in the room (right) hides a feeling (left). This one is for your notes, not the client's wall.
diagrams.evidenceNote: The two triangles are a durable clinical heuristic from dynamic psychotherapy, taught widely; they organise inference, not data, and carry the interpretive risks of that tradition.

diagrams.oneLiner: A personal crisis plan: warning signs, steps to take, and who to call — with no dead ends.
diagrams.whatItShows: A navigable plan for hard moments — warning signs, self-soothing steps, reasons for living, people and services to contact, and means-safety — laid out so every branch leads somewhere and a crisis line is always one step away. It is the client's, to keep and use.
diagrams.whenToUse: When there is risk to plan for: to co-write a safety plan the person actually holds, rehearses, and can follow when distress narrows their thinking.
diagrams.onPaper: Write it as a numbered list the person can follow when overwhelmed: (1) signs I am slipping, (2) things that help me cope alone, (3) people and places that distract and support, (4) who to call, (5) how to make my environment safer. Put a real crisis number at the top and bottom. Keep a copy in their phone.
diagrams.evidenceNote: Safety planning has supporting evidence as a brief intervention and is not the same as a no-harm contract (which is not evidence-based). A diagram never replaces clinical risk assessment and local crisis services.

diagrams.oneLiner: Feared situations ranked by difficulty, hardest at the top, with where to start.
diagrams.whatItShows: An exposure hierarchy: feared situations rated by anticipated distress (a 0–100 SUDS rating) and stacked as rungs, hardest at the top. The lower rungs are where exposure begins, so the ladder is both a plan and a record of progress as rungs get easier.
diagrams.whenToUse: Whenever graded exposure is the method — phobias, OCD, social anxiety, agoraphobia, PTSD avoidance — to plan a doable sequence and to show that approach, not avoidance, shrinks fear.
diagrams.onPaper: List the avoided situations, then ask for a 0–100 'how hard right now?' on each and sort them into a ladder, hardest at the top. Pick a low rung to start. Re-rate after each attempt — watching the numbers fall is the point.
diagrams.evidenceNote: Exposure is among the best-evidenced techniques in psychotherapy; the ladder is its planning tool. Distress ratings are subjective and shift — they guide pacing, they do not measure pathology.

diagrams.oneLiner: Life domains plotted by how close the person is living to what matters — darts on a target.
diagrams.whatItShows: A target whose centre is 'living fully by my values'. In each life domain (work, relationships, leisure, health, growth) the person places a dart: near the centre means on-target, out at the rim means adrift. The spread of darts is the picture — where life is and is not aligned with values.
diagrams.whenToUse: In ACT to clarify values versus goals, to spot where action has drifted from what matters, and to choose a committed-action direction without making it a self-criticism exercise.
diagrams.onPaper: Draw a dartboard with a few rings. Quarter it into life areas. In each area, put a dot for how close you are living to what you care about — bullseye is bang-on, rim is far off. Then pick one dart to nudge inwards and name one small action.
diagrams.evidenceNote: ACT has a solid evidence base; the bull's-eye is a values-clarification worksheet within it. Dart positions are self-rated reflections, not scores — and 'off target' is information, not failure.

diagrams.oneLiner: A 2×2 of changing versus staying, against benefits and costs — ambivalence made visible.
diagrams.whatItShows: A four-cell grid: benefits of changing, costs of changing, benefits of staying the same, and costs of staying. Filling all four lays ambivalence out honestly rather than arguing one side. It is a reflection tool, used with care so it does not become persuasion.
diagrams.whenToUse: When a person is genuinely two-minded about a change and wants to think it through — explicitly NOT to push a predetermined direction (MI cautions that decisional balance can backfire when change is the goal).
diagrams.onPaper: Quarter the page. Label: change → good things / not-so-good things; stay the same → good things / not-so-good things. Fill every box in the person's own words. Resist tidying it toward your preferred answer — the point is their clarity, not your case.
diagrams.evidenceNote: Decisional balance is a classic MI / stages-of-change tool; MI's own developers caution it can entrench ambivalence if used to drive change, so it suits true deliberation, not persuasion. It is a reflection, not an assessment.

diagrams.school: Anthropology of ritual (van Gennep; Turner); therapeutic ritual
diagrams.oneLiner: A marked transition in three phases — leaving the old, the threshold between, arriving at the new.
diagrams.whatItShows: A ceremonial or symbolic transition structured into van Gennep's three phases — separation, liminal threshold, reincorporation — each phase holding the acts that carry the person across. It is used to mark endings, losses, recoveries and identity shifts deliberately rather than letting them pass unnamed.
diagrams.whenToUse: To co-design a therapeutic ritual (an ending of therapy, a memorial, a marking of recovery or a new identity), where a structured, meaningful transition helps more than talk alone.
diagrams.onPaper: Fold or rule the page into three columns: leaving · threshold · arriving. In each, write the acts that belong there — what is set down, what is crossed, what is taken up. Honesty matters here: name the framing openly and offer a secular version, so no one is asked to perform a belief that is not theirs.
diagrams.evidenceNote: Therapeutic ritual draws on anthropology and clinical practice rather than trial evidence. It must be consent-based and culturally careful — a ritual can carry meanings the clinician does not hold; never improvise sacred forms.
